title: 📰 AI news · November 4
cta: 🔐 Check where my keys are stored
takeaway: Today's news is about keys, passwords and access: they get stolen from companies and from people, and the owner pays. Recommendation: check where your bot's keys are stored and when you last changed the passwords in your password manager.

items.title: Stolen AI keys are being resold
items.text: Google says hackers steal keys and tokens from unprotected computers and resell access to AI models. The key owner pays: some organizations were billed over $100,000 a day. If you run a bot or an agent on AI, its keys sit in the same kind of settings. Check where your bot's keys are stored: in code, in notes or in chats. Free guide "Protecting your computer, code and access" — send the word "protect" to the bot.

items.title: Chainstack was breached through a third-party component
items.text: Attackers got into the development environment, reached production and saw customer emails and password hashes. The company treats node access keys as exposed. If your bot or site runs on someone else's platform, its breach can open your keys too. Check which keys each service you use holds for you.

items.title: Password manager mSecure asks users to change passwords
items.text: The company emailed customers about suspicious activity and suggests changing passwords, resetting two-factor protection and removing passkeys. What exactly happened is not yet disclosed. If your passwords live in a service like this, they guard all your accounts at once. Look at which passwords you changed in the last month.

items.title: Ransomware is encrypting Synology storage
items.text: The C3RB3R ransomware attacks home Synology storage running an old DSM version and demands a ransom. It uses a flaw that was fixed in late 2024. If you keep projects and client files on such a device, they are at risk. Check your DSM version and turn on automatic updates.

items.title: GPT-6 Astra designed a device in under a week
items.text: OpenAI's model made the enclosure, board, firmware and interface of a device for talking to Codex. A factory produced prototypes in under a month. AI is starting to design hardware, not only text and code.

items.title: Claude answers faster in long conversations
items.text: Anthropic launched Message Threads: a request now carries only what changed since the last message. Time to first token on requests of 500,000 tokens and more dropped by about 35%. Coding agents and work with large documents benefit most.

items.title: Claude Code stopped recreating existing games
items.text: Two sentences in the Opus 5.5 system prompt forbid rebuilding existing games, even renamed ones. Original games with your own assets are still fine. The rule followed a wave of unofficial ports of Halo and GTA Vice City.

items.title: A rigid beam was 3D-printed in orbit
items.text: The Replicator 2 satellite from Germany's Orbital Matter printed a half-meter beam in space. Engineers think beams up to 100 meters are possible. Such structures are needed for large solar arrays on future satellites.

items.title: Netflix adds an AI tab that picks by mood
items.text: You choose a theme like "something light" or "scare me" and get a selection. The tab starts in the US on TVs, with a wider rollout in the coming weeks.

items.title: Apple closes dating and AI companion apps to under-18s
items.text: Dating apps and AI companions with romantic content now get an 18+ rating, including Character.AI and Replika. Developers add the new content descriptors from November 16.

items.title: Honor is preparing a phone that lasts a week
items.text: Per rumors, the phone has a 14,000–15,000 mAh battery that has entered trial production. A launch is expected next year.
